notes: Ruling slot 4 = PCC (Castro). MD's 'PCC wings' in 0 and 19 replaced: 0 = RECE exile organisation, 19 = Guevarist 'Hombre Nuevo' line; 6 = Escalante's Microfracción (pro-Soviet hardliners); 7 = MININT. Exile parties fill the Western slots; Alpha 66 in 20, Cuban Nationalist Movement in 21. MD sprites kept only for PCC (4) and FAR (22).

0.name: Representación Cubana del Exilio
0.text:
Cuban Representation in Exile is an anti-Castro exile organisation founded in Miami in 1964, financed by wealthy émigrés and promoted by its young spokesman Jorge Mas Canosa, a veteran of the Bay of Pigs brigade. On 1 January 1970 it raises funds, lobbies Washington and backs commando raids against the Cuban coast.

It seeks the overthrow of Fidel Castro and a provisional government under strong anti-communist leadership, followed by the return of property and a market economy closely tied to the United States. It cares more for order than for elections. Its leverage lies in exile money, contacts in Congress and the intelligence services, and the backing of Miami business.

1.name: Movimiento Demócrata Cristiano de Cuba
1.text:
The Christian Democratic Movement of Cuba was founded in 1959 by José Ignacio Rasco and other Catholic lay leaders who had backed the struggle against Batista but broke with Castro over communism. Its members fought at the Bay of Pigs, and on 1 January 1970 it lives in exile in Miami, Caracas and San Juan.

It calls for a democratic, Catholic-inspired Cuba under the 1940 Constitution, with a social market economy, land for peasants and freedom for the Church. It is anti-communist but wary of Batistiano revanchism. Its leverage lies in links with Latin American Christian Democrats, above all in Venezuela and Chile, and with Catholic exiles.

2.name: Los Constitucionalistas del 40
2.text:
Los Constitucionalistas del 40 are the exiled lawyers, judges, professors and former legislators who make the 1940 Constitution their banner. Many served the elected governments of the 1940s or opposed Batista's 1952 coup, then left Cuba when Castro postponed elections indefinitely. On 1 January 1970 they gather in the exile professional associations and university circles of Miami.

They demand a return to constitutional rule, free elections, independent courts, a free press and compensation for confiscated property under the rule of law. Liberal and anti-communist, they reject both Castro and the Batistiano option. Their leverage lies in legal prestige, exile institutions and the moral authority of the constitution itself.

3.name: Partido Revolucionario Cubano (Auténtico)
3.text:
The Authentic Party is the Cuban Revolutionary Party (Authentic), founded in 1934 by followers of Ramón Grau San Martín and in power from 1944 to 1952 under Grau and Carlos Prío Socarrás. Overthrown by Batista's 1952 coup, its leaders first backed and then broke with Castro; on 1 January 1970 Prío leads its remnant in Miami exile.

It stands for the reformist nationalism of the 1933 revolution: labour rights, social security, agrarian reform and the 1940 Constitution, within parliamentary democracy and alliance with the United States. Its base is older exiles, former unionists and professionals, and its leverage lies in its historic name and networks.

4.name: Partido Comunista de Cuba
4.text:
The Communist Party of Cuba is the ruling party, constituted in October 1965 from the earlier union of Castro's 26th of July Movement, the Popular Socialist Party and the Revolutionary Directorate. Fidel Castro is First Secretary and Prime Minister, Raúl Castro Second Secretary and Osvaldo Dorticós President. On 1 January 1970 the whole country is mobilised for the Ten Million Ton sugar harvest.

The party holds absolute power, has not yet held a congress and governs through Castro's personal authority and mass rallies. It pursues a radical socialism of moral incentives, voluntary labour and armed internationalism, while depending on Soviet oil, credit and arms. Its leverage is total control of the state, economy and media.

5.name: Organización Tricontinental
5.english: Organization of Solidarity with the People of Asia, Africa and Latin America
5.native_full: Organización de Solidaridad con los Pueblos de Asia, África y América Latina
5.text:
The Organization of Solidarity with the People of Asia, Africa and Latin America was created in Havana at the Tricontinental Conference of January 1966 to unite liberation movements against imperialism. On 1 January 1970 it publishes the Tricontinental magazine and its striking posters, and keeps Havana the meeting place of guerrillas from Vietnam to Guinea-Bissau.

It preaches Che Guevara's call to create two, three, many Vietnams, armed struggle over electoral roads and solidarity among the poor nations. It is often at odds with Moscow's caution and with orthodox communist parties in Latin America. Its leverage lies in Cuban backing, training camps and revolutionary prestige.

6.name: La Microfracción
6.text:
La Microfracción is the name given to the old Popular Socialist Party militants around Aníbal Escalante who were tried in January 1968 for conspiring with Soviet and East German officials against Castro's line. Escalante was sentenced to fifteen years in prison; on 1 January 1970 his circle is broken, but its outlook survives among orthodox cadres.

It stands for Soviet-style orthodoxy: party rule over the guerrilla commanders, material incentives, central planning on the Moscow model and an end to adventurist exports of revolution. It despises Guevarism as petty-bourgeois romanticism. Its leverage lies in Moscow's growing economic hold over Cuba.

7.name: Ministerio del Interior
7.text:
The Ministry of the Interior is the security apparatus of the revolution, led by Commander Sergio del Valle Jiménez. It combines State Security, the National Revolutionary Police, the border guards and the General Intelligence Directorate under Manuel Piñeiro, which supports guerrillas across Latin America. On 1 January 1970 it is at the height of its power.

Its officers, many trained by the Soviet KGB, watch over counter-revolutionaries, dissidents and exile infiltrators, and it holds thousands of political prisoners. Loyal to Fidel personally, its leverage lies in surveillance, prisons, intelligence networks abroad and control over who may leave the island.

8.name: Los Becarios de Tiro
8.text:
Los Becarios de Tiro are Lebanese Shia students from southern Lebanon studying in Havana on Cuban scholarships granted to progressive Arab organisations. On 1 January 1970 they form a tiny circle that keeps its faith discreetly within the secular student residences.

They are drawn to Musa al-Sadr's movement for the dignity of the deprived Shia of the Lebanese south and favour a reformist, socially engaged Islam compatible with anti-imperialism. They avoid open conflict with Cuban atheism and stay outside Cuban politics. Their influence is confined to their own community and its contacts with Lebanese organisations.

9.name: Los Discípulos de Nayaf
9.text:
Los Discípulos de Nayaf are a handful of Iraqi Shia students in Havana who quietly pass around writings from the seminaries of Najaf, including the ideas of the Islamic Da'wa Party and of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf. On 1 January 1970 they are invisible in Cuban public life.

They reject both Soviet atheism and American power, condemn the Shah and Ba'athist secularism alike, and dream of an Islamic order led by the clergy. Their presence in revolutionary Havana is a paradox they keep to themselves. Their leverage in Cuba is nil, resting only on devotion and links to clerical networks abroad.

10.name: Los Azharíes de La Habana
10.text:
Los Azharíes de La Habana are the Egyptian, Algerian and other Arab diplomats, teachers and technicians in Havana who follow the official Islam of Cairo's Al-Azhar. On 1 January 1970 they gather for Friday prayers in embassy rooms and private homes, the only organised Muslim worship on the island.

Their Islam is establishment and quietist: loyalty to their own governments, personal piety and avoidance of political agitation. They respect their Cuban hosts and keep religion out of public view. Their leverage lies in diplomatic status and the friendship between Havana and the progressive Arab republics.

11.name: Los Estudiantes del Califato
11.text:
Los Estudiantes del Califato is a handful of Palestinian and Jordanian students in Havana, sent by liberation organisations, who have privately come into contact with Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani. On 1 January 1970 they meet in secret and conceal their views from their Marxist comrades.

They regard every existing state as illegitimate and call for the restoration of a single caliphate for all Muslims. Hostile to Israel, the United States and Soviet atheism alike, they reject parties and elections. Their only assets are conviction and contact with the party's cells in the Middle East.

12.name: Los Hermanos de Jartum
12.text:
Los Hermanos de Jartum are a few Sudanese and other Arab students in Havana who sympathise with the Muslim Brotherhood and with Hasan al-Turabi's Islamic Charter Front, banned after Jaafar Nimeiry's coup in May 1969. On 1 January 1970 they meet discreetly for prayer and study of Sayyid Qutb.

They call for the moral renewal of society through preaching, education and charity, and hope for Islamic government achieved by gradual means. They oppose Zionism, Western materialism and communist atheism, which places them quietly at odds with their hosts. Their leverage is limited to student solidarity and links to the Brotherhood abroad.

13.name: Junta Central de Planificación
13.text:
The Central Planning Board is the technocratic heart of the Cuban economy, created in 1960 to draw up plans for every sector. On 1 January 1970 its economists and engineers are struggling as the Ten Million Ton harvest swallows labour, transport and fuel, and annual plans give way to Fidel's direct campaigns.

Its planners want realistic targets, sound accounting, material incentives and closer integration with Soviet planning, without surrendering Cuba's independence. They are neither guerrilla romantics nor party ideologues but managers of scarcity. Their leverage lies in statistics, expertise and the realism that the strained economy will soon demand.

14.name: Iglesia Católica en Cuba
14.text:
The Catholic Church in Cuba survived the confrontation of 1960-1961, when priests were expelled and Catholic schools nationalised, as a small and cautious institution. On 1 January 1970 it is led by Havana's Archbishop Evelio Díaz Cía and guided by the Vatican's envoy Monsignor Cesare Zacchi, who seeks coexistence with the revolution.

In April 1969 the bishops denounced the American economic blockade, signalling a search for dialogue. The Church defends religious freedom, the family and Catholic education, and quietly shelters believers excluded from university and party careers. Its leverage lies in moral authority, rural devotion and its link to Rome.

15.name: Los Hacendados del Exilio
15.text:
Los Hacendados del Exilio are the sugar barons, cattle ranchers and industrialists whose mills, estates and companies were nationalised in 1959 and 1960 and who now live in Miami, New York, Madrid and Santo Domingo. Families such as the Fanjuls are rebuilding sugar fortunes in Florida, while others keep detailed claims to their Cuban property.

They demand the return of or compensation for confiscated assets, the end of state farms and a Cuba open again to private and American capital. Fiercely anti-communist, they finance exile politics and lobby in Washington. Their leverage lies in money, legal claims in US courts and ties to American agribusiness.

16.name: Cámara de Comercio Latina de los Estados Unidos
16.english: Latin Chamber of Commerce of the United States
16.native_full: Cámara de Comercio Latina de los Estados Unidos
16.text:
The Latin Chamber of Commerce of the United States was founded in Miami in 1965 by Cuban exile businessmen building new lives in Little Havana. On 1 January 1970 it represents a fast-growing class of exile shopkeepers, builders, bankers and traders who are turning the Cuban community into an economic force in South Florida.

It preaches free enterprise and self-reliance as the answer to communism and envisions a future Cuba rebuilt by private initiative with minimal state interference. It supports American policy against Castro. Its leverage lies in the commercial success of exile Miami and its contacts with American business and local politics.

17.name: Academia de Ciencias de Cuba
17.text:
The Cuban Academy of Sciences was refounded in 1962 under the geographer and cave explorer Antonio Núñez Jiménez, a veteran of Che Guevara's column. On 1 January 1970 it oversees research institutes, expeditions and surveys of Cuba's caves, swamps, forests and coasts, including the great Zapata Swamp.

Its scientists press for nature reserves, reforestation, protection of rare species such as the Cuban crocodile and rational use of natural resources within socialist planning. Loyal to the revolution, they still warn about the ecological cost of drainage and sugar monoculture. Their leverage lies in scientific authority and Núñez Jiménez's closeness to Fidel.

18.name: Vergüenza contra Dinero
18.text:
Vergüenza contra Dinero, Eduardo Chibás's slogan, names the surviving tradition of the Orthodox Party, the anti-corruption movement whose youth wing produced Fidel Castro. Dissolved in the revolution, its veterans are divided on 1 January 1970: some serve the new state, while others, like its former presidential candidate Roberto Agramonte, live in exile.

They uphold the original promise of the struggle against Batista: social justice, honest government, national sovereignty and the 1940 Constitution, without Soviet tutelage or renewed American domination. They see the revolution as captured by the communists. Their leverage lies in the moral prestige of Chibás's name on both sides of the Florida Straits.

19.name: El Hombre Nuevo
19.text:
El Hombre Nuevo is the Guevarist line within the revolutionary leadership, named after Che Guevara's ideal of a new socialist human being. Since Che's death in Bolivia in 1967 it has become official creed: on 1 January 1970 moral incentives, voluntary labour and the near-abolition of money drive the Ten Million Ton harvest.

Its followers believe Cuba can build communism directly, skipping the Soviet stage of material incentives and markets, and must spread revolution through the Third World independently of Moscow. They prize sacrifice over efficiency and revolutionary will over planning. Their leverage lies in Fidel's own enthusiasm and the energy of the youth brigades.

20.name: Alpha 66
20.text:
Alpha 66 is a militant exile organisation founded in the early 1960s by veterans of the anti-Batista struggle, among them Eloy Gutiérrez Menoyo and Antonio Veciana. Gutiérrez Menoyo was captured after landing in Cuba in 1964 and sits in a Cuban prison; on 1 January 1970 the group, led from Miami by Andrés Nazario Sargén, trains commandos in Florida and raids the Cuban coast.

It rallies working- and middle-class exiles with fiery nationalism, rejects both communism and a return of the Batistianos, and promises a free, sovereign and socially just Cuba won by Cubans themselves. Its leverage lies in armed raids, radio broadcasts and exile street support.

21.name: Movimiento Nacionalista Cubano
21.text:
The Cuban Nationalist Movement is a small, violent exile organisation founded in the early 1960s by Felipe Rivero Díaz, a Bay of Pigs prisoner released in 1962. On 1 January 1970 its cells in Miami, New Jersey and New York are known for bombings of targets linked to Castro's Cuba and to countries that trade with it.

It preaches an ultranationalist, authoritarian and Catholic integralist creed modelled on European fascism, with contempt for liberal democracy and for exiles it considers soft. It sees violence as the only path to a reborn Cuba. Its leverage lies in a cadre of hardened militants and fear within the exile community itself.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias
22.text:
The Revolutionary Armed Forces grew out of Castro's Rebel Army and are commanded by Raúl Castro as Minister of the Armed Forces. Equipped with Soviet tanks and MiG fighters and among the largest forces in Latin America, they defeated the Bay of Pigs invasion, and on 1 January 1970 their soldiers are also cutting cane for the Ten Million Ton harvest.

The FAR embodies the revolution's guerrilla legend and its growing professionalism under Soviet advisers. Its officers value discipline, organisation and loyalty to the Castro brothers, and they train guerrillas from Africa and Latin America. Its leverage lies in arms, prestige and its role as the backbone of the state.

23.name: Los Leales de la Capitanía
23.text:
Los Leales de la Capitanía are a small circle of elderly exiles in Madrid and Miami, descendants of Spanish loyalist families who still regard the Captaincy General of Cuba, lost in 1898, as the island's golden age. On 1 January 1970 they meet in Hispanic cultural societies and Catholic associations without any political organisation.

They argue that a Catholic monarchy bound to Spain would bring order after the chaos of the republic and the revolution, and they welcome Franco's 1969 designation of Juan Carlos de Borbón as his successor. Their influence is limited to memoirs, ceremonies and nostalgic polemics in exile newspapers.
